Northwind emailed Marco on Sunday night reporting that their invoices had exported with the wrong tax rate for their Dutch entity, and their finance team only caught it after some had already been sent to clients. [[M1#16]]

**Cause:** Diego traced it to the rounding change made in August, which only affected accounts with multiple tax jurisdictions — essentially just Northwind. [[M1#17]]

**Scope:** 41 invoices over two weeks. Diego said the calculation fix was quick, but regenerating the PDFs was the awkward part since they had already gone out. [[M1#19]]

**Response:** Marco had Diego fix it the same day and send Northwind a note listing the affected invoice numbers so they could send corrections, while Marco called their CFO himself. [[M1#20]] Diego committed to the fix that day and the list by the next morning. [[M1#21]] Marco instructed that no credit be promised in the note; he would decide after the call. [[M1#23]]

**Resolution:** By the September 15 sync the issue was closed — corrected invoices went out, Northwind's finance team confirmed the numbers, and the CFO replied to Marco's note. [[M2#9]] Marco gave them one month free and asked Ana to apply the credit that day. [[M2#10]][[M2#11]] At the retro Diego called it a win: a bad week, fixed in a day, and the customer stayed. [[M4#2]]

Ana leads the pricing page redesign — Marco stated the decision in the September 1 Q4 planning meeting: "the pricing page redesign ships in Q4, Ana leads it, and the target is end of September." [[M1#7]] Ana produced the mockups (three tiers, annual billing toggle, comparison table below the fold) and owns the build once the copy is approved [[M1#3]][[M1#5]].

She has stayed the owner since: she reported the legal-copy delay and committed to the new October 15 launch date [[M3#3]], presented the page at the September 22 design review with Priya [[M2#0]], and took the resulting action items (updated mockups by Thursday, anchor links, enterprise line, free-tier price display) [[M2#12]][[M2#17]][[M2#23]][[M2#25]].

No. Marco decided in Q4 planning on September 1: no mobile app in Q4, to be revisited in January if the mobile session share changes. [[M1#25]] The reasoning was that only about eight percent of sessions are on a phone, and most of those are people checking invoice status, which the responsive site already handles [[M1#23]], and building it would consume the whole quarter for two people [[M1#24]].

Marco restated it on September 8: the mobile app is not happening, January at the earliest, despite ongoing support requests. [[M4#25]] Sofía was to add a note to the support macro so the team stops promising it [[M1#26]], and to link Marco's written roadmap statement from that macro [[M4#26]].

At the September 29 retro, Marco confirmed the cut stood with "zero regrets," saying every support request made him more confident because the people asking want a feature the responsive site already has. [[M2#23]]

**Drata**, decided at the September 29 retro. [[M1#18]][[M1#19]]

Marco presented three quotes — Vanta, Drata, and Secureframe — all within twenty percent of each other on price. Drata had the best Postgres and GitHub integrations, which cover most of the team's evidence collection; Vanta had a nicer dashboard, and Secureframe was cheapest but had a smaller auditor network. [[M1#16]] Diego, who has to feed the platform, argued integrations matter more than the dashboard, and Sofía agreed on Drata. [[M1#17]][[M1#18]]

Note that the vendor field widened along the way: on September 1 the evaluation was scoped to just Vanta and Drata [[M2#22]], but Marco ultimately brought three quotes to the retro [[M1#16]].

Next steps from that decision: Marco signs in the first week of October, and Diego kicks off the integrations after the checkout change ships, so late October. [[M1#19]] The audit itself is Q1, since evidence collection takes three months minimum. [[M1#22]]

Fifteen percent. Marco reported that finance wanted the annual discount cut from the twenty percent shown on the page to fifteen [[M1#6]], a change that came down on the Friday before the September 22 design review, on the grounds that the original twenty percent — a number Marco says he made up two years earlier — cost more than it brought in [[M1#8]]. Marco confirmed it as a decision and said he'd absorb the complaints [[M1#11]].

On presentation: Priya argued the saving should be shown in currency, not only percent, since "Save 96 dollars a year" lands harder than "15 percent" [[M1#9]]. The agreed treatment is both — percent on the annual toggle, the currency amount under each price [[M1#10]][[M1#11]]. Ana was to update the mockups with the new fifteen percent discount by Thursday [[M1#12]].

The drop-off is concentrated at the **billing address step** in the checkout funnel.

- **Sept 1:** Sofía only knew that roughly a third of people were lost between picking a plan and confirming payment, with no visibility into which step, because the funnel events weren't granular enough [[M1#10]]. Diego guessed it was the address form, since a full billing address is requested even for card payments and Stripe doesn't need it [[M1#11]].
- **Sept 8:** After Diego shipped the funnel events [[M3#10]], the early data confirmed his guess: the biggest drop was at the billing address step, with 28% of people who pick a plan leaving on that screen [[M3#11]].
- **Sept 15 (most recent figure):** With two more weeks of data, the number settled at a **29% drop at the billing address step**, flat across plans and countries [[M2#1]].

That led to the decision to remove the address step for card payments while keeping it for bank transfer and invoice-based plans, shipping one week after the pricing page (around October 22) [[M2#1]][[M2#6]].
